item.title: S3E7 · Full Book Review — The Guns of August
item.description: A closing conversation on the book as a whole: what Tuchman's month-by-month narrative argues about how wars actually begin, why her account of 1914 became required reading during the Cuban Missile Crisis, and what still holds up — and what doesn't — six decades on.
item.content:encoded:
A closing conversation on The Guns of August as a whole: what Tuchman's month-by-month narrative argues about how wars actually begin — not through anyone's clear intention, but through rigid plans, tight timetables, and leaders who kept moving even after they doubted the wisdom of it.

We also talk about the book's afterlife: why it became required reading in the Kennedy White House during the Cuban Missile Crisis, and which parts of the argument still hold up sixty years on.

item.title: S3E1 · Overview — The Guns of August
item.description: Barbara Tuchman's 1962 Pulitzer Prize–winning account of how the great powers stumbled from the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand into a continental war within five weeks — bound by mobilization timetables and war plans drawn up years in advance. A full-book discussion of the July crisis, the invasion of Belgium, and the battles of the war's first month that set the terms for everything that followed.
item.content:encoded:
Barbara Tuchman's The Guns of August (1962) won the Pulitzer Prize for its account of how the great powers stumbled from the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand into a continental war within five weeks — bound by mobilization timetables and war plans drawn up years in advance, chief among them the German Schlieffen Plan and the French Plan XVII.

This first episode takes the book whole: the funeral of Edward VII that opens it, the diplomatic collapse of July 1914, the invasion of Belgium, and the battles of the war's first month that decided the shape of everything that followed.

Season 3 continues with the front matter, three chapter-by-chapter episodes, the end matter, and a closing full-book review.

item.title: S1E1 · Overview — The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam
item.description: Barbara Tuchman's 1984 study of governments that pursue policies squarely against their own interest — the Trojans hauling the horse inside the walls, the Renaissance popes provoking the Protestant secession, Britain losing America, and America in Vietnam. A full-book discussion of what she means by folly, the four tests she sets for it, and whether the pattern really holds.
item.content:encoded:
Barbara Tuchman's The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (1984) asks a deceptively simple question: why do governments so often pursue policies that run directly against their own interests, when a better course was both available and argued for at the time?

This first episode takes the book whole. We work through her four case studies — the Trojans hauling the horse inside the walls, the Renaissance popes provoking the Protestant secession, Britain losing America, and America in Vietnam — and then test the framework itself: the four criteria she sets for folly, why she insists on contemporary rather than hindsight judgment, and where the argument strains.

Season 1 continues with chapter and thematic episodes on the same book.
